name: Las Palmas
title: Las Palmas UTM: Hull, Rig & Tank Thickness Measurement
description: Thickness measurement in Las Palmas for ships and offshore rigs: hull structure gauging, pre-docking survey readings and renewal survey UTM on Gran Canaria
h1: Ultrasonic Thickness Measurement for Ships and Rigs in Las Palmas
intro: The Port of Las Palmas is the Atlantic stop between Europe, West Africa and South America: a bunkering hub, a base for fishing and reefer fleets, and a ship-repair and lay-up port where drilling rigs and offshore vessels come in from West African fields. Long yard and lay-by stays make it one of the better places in the region for structured gauging. We mobilise technicians from India to Gran Canaria for ships, rigs and offshore units, planned around the yard period or the rig's work window.

highlights.p: Jack-ups, semi-submersibles and offshore vessels come to Las Palmas between West African contracts. We gauge legs, columns, pontoons and tanks to a plan agreed with class, working under the operator's permits.

Repair periods at Astican and lay-ups in the outer harbour give time for tank-by-tank measurement, following the yard's cleaning sequence and adding post-blast confirmation where the surveyor asks for it.
Ships diverting to the islands for fuel can use the stop for targeted readings — a suspect tank, a piping line or pre-purchase sampling — scoped to the hours the ship will actually stay.

port.h: Las Palmas: Atlantic bunkering, fishing fleets and rig stays
p: The Puerto de La Luz y de Las Palmas, run by the Autoridad Portuaria de Las Palmas, sits on the main sea routes between Europe and the South Atlantic and close to the West African coast. That position has made it one of the principal bunkering ports in the eastern Atlantic, with ships diverting from passage to take fuel at the quays or at anchor. Container lines use it to tranship cargo for West Africa and the islands, and it has long been a base for international fishing fleets and the reefers that carry their catch.

The port's second identity is ship repair and lay-up. Drilling rigs, jack-ups and offshore support vessels working off West Africa come to Las Palmas between contracts for maintenance, inspection and stacking, alongside merchant ships taking repair periods at Astican and with the other repair firms in the port. Laid-up merchant ships also wait out weak markets here, sometimes for long periods, and return to service only after surveys that need gauging. In winter the cruise season adds another layer, with ships on Canary Islands and transatlantic itineraries calling regularly. The result is a port where some ships stay for hours and others for weeks or months.

For thickness gauging, the long stays are what matter. A rig stacked between contracts or an offshore vessel in for its renewal survey can be gauged systematically, tank by tank, with time for cleaning, ventilation and access, which makes hull gauging in Las Palmas closer to yard work than to a port call. Fishing vessels and reefers working from the port face hard service — ice, brine, fish-hold wear and long periods at sea — and their owners use the stays here for structural checks. Offshore support vessels, standby vessels and tugs from the West African oil and gas sector use the port for docking and class work as well, while ships stopping only for bunkers offer short windows that suit targeted readings.

facilities.h: Astican, the rig quays and the bunker berths: gauging sites in Las Palmas
p: Ship-repair work centres on Astican, whose docking facilities handle merchant ships, fishing vessels and offshore units, and on the repair companies that work afloat along the port's quays. In a repair period, gauging is usually the first job: readings in tanks, holds and on external shell set the steel renewal scope, and a second round after cleaning or blasting confirms which areas need cropping and renewal. Reefers and fishing vessels lie alongside the fishing and cold-store quays, where holds, tanks and decks can be gauged between trips.

Rigs and large offshore units lie at lay-by quays in the outer harbour, sometimes for long periods. Work on them needs the operator's permit-to-work system, access to legs, columns, pontoons, preload and ballast tanks, and a measurement plan agreed with class before measuring starts. Rig and offshore work often runs over several weeks, and the number of technicians and the schedule are adjusted as cleaning and access open new areas. For ships at anchor or calling for bunkers, launches are booked through the ship's agent, and the trade winds and Atlantic swell can affect boarding in the outer anchorage, so a margin in the schedule is sensible.
list: Astican shipyard — docking and renewal survey gauging of hull, tanks and holds on merchant ships, fishing vessels and offshore support vessels
Rig lay-by quays in the outer harbour — gauging of legs, columns, pontoons, preload and ballast tanks on jack-ups and semi-submersibles between contracts
Bunkering berths and anchorage — targeted gauging and pre-purchase sampling on ships stopping for fuel on Atlantic passages
Fishing and cold-store quays — fish-hold, tank and deck gauging on fishing vessels and reefers between trips
Container and cruise berths — scrubber and sea-water piping gauging on container ships and winter-season cruise ships during calls
Afloat repair quays — gauging alongside repair crews so steel renewal and piping replacement can be planned within the same stay

context.h: Canary Islands context: flags, fuel rules and the West Africa link
p: The Canary Islands are part of Spain and of the EU, so Las Palmas applies Spanish port state control under the Paris MoU, EU at-berth sulphur rules, EU ETS for shipping since 2024 and FuelEU Maritime since 2025. No SOx ECA covers the islands' waters, and ships here burn fuel meeting the global sulphur limit at sea or run scrubbers on high-sulphur fuel. Spain's second ship register, the Canary Islands Special Register, takes its name from the islands, and many Spanish-flag merchant ships are entered in it.

Commercially, Las Palmas is tied to West Africa. Offshore drilling and production campaigns in the Gulf of Guinea and off Mauritania and Senegal drive demand for offshore rig inspection and maintenance here, and the periods between contracts are when owners schedule class renewal work on their units. The same link brings ships that have spent long periods in warm, humid trades, where ballast tank coatings and deck structure deteriorate faster, and owners often use a stop in the islands to measure the extent of the damage before deciding where to dock. For a manager whose ship is already in the Atlantic, gauging in Las Palmas can settle that question before the ship heads north to Europe or south again.

jobs.h: Las Palmas gauging work, from bunker calls to stacked rigs
jobs.p: Las Palmas jobs range from a few hours on a bunkering ship to weeks on a stacked rig. The longer the stay, the more systematic the work can be; on rigs and ships in repair periods, the technicians often follow the yard's cleaning sequence, measuring each space as it is released. Each job starts with a measurement plan agreed with the owner and, for survey work, presented to the attending surveyor. Typical requests:
list: Rig thickness measurement on a jack-up stacked in the outer harbour between West African contracts: legs, preload tanks and hull structure gauged ahead of its class renewal.
Renewal survey gauging of an offshore supply vessel docked at Astican, covering bottom shell, ballast and fuel tanks, decks and frames, with post-blast confirmation readings.
Fish-hold and deck gauging on a reefer or fishing vessel between trips, checking wastage where ice, brine and handling gear have attacked the structure.
Pre-purchase gauging of a bulk carrier during a bunkering call, sampling deck, hold and ballast tank structure to support a buyer's decision before the ship leaves the islands.
Reactivation gauging of a merchant ship coming out of lay-up, measuring tanks and piping that have stood idle so that class and the owner can plan the return to service.

logistics: Gran Canaria Airport is the entry point, normally reached from India through Madrid or a similar European connection, with a short road transfer to the port. The Canary Islands are in the Schengen area, so technicians travel on Schengen visas, and we fix travel dates once those visas are issued and the yard period or the rig's work window is confirmed. Yard access is arranged with the shipyard, rig access with the operator, and ISPS passes or launches through the ship's agent. Long rig and repair stays usually allow all of this to be planned well ahead.

faqs.q: Can you gauge a drilling rig stacked in Las Palmas?
faqs.a: Yes. We measure hull, deck, leg and column structure and tanks on jack-ups and semi-submersibles using ultrasonic gauges, with magnetic particle testing at nodes and other fatigue-prone details where required. The work is run under the operator's permit-to-work system and to a measurement plan agreed with class, and is usually spread over several weeks as spaces are opened and cleaned.

faqs.q: Is Las Palmas inside an emission control area?
faqs.a: Not at present. The Canary Islands lie outside the Mediterranean and North Sea ECAs, so on passage ships comply with the global sulphur cap through compliant fuel or a scrubber. Alongside in Las Palmas, the EU's in-port sulphur requirement applies unless an equivalent abatement method is in use. Scrubber-fitted container and cruise ships calling here still run their systems on passage, and their piping benefits from regular ultrasonic checks.

faqs.q: Can gauging be done on a fishing vessel between trips?
faqs.a: Yes. Fishing vessels and reefers working from Las Palmas spend short periods alongside between trips, and fish holds, tanks and decks can be gauged then if the crew empties and cleans the spaces in advance. Insulated fish holds limit access to the shell from inside, so we agree with the owner which areas can be reached and whether readings from outside during a docking are needed.

faqs.q: What happens if gauging finds substantial corrosion during a repair period at Astican?
faqs.a: We report the readings against the allowable diminution, marking areas of substantial and excessive corrosion so the surveyor and the yard can agree renewals or additional close-up survey. Because the technicians are already on site, follow-up readings in areas opened up by cropping or blasting can be taken while the yard is still working on them, which keeps the repair period moving.
